records.name: Imperial Palace
records.description: The main residence of the Emperor of Japan, built on the former site of Edo Castle in central Chiyoda. The grounds hold the Kyuden ceremonial palace and the Fukiage imperial residence; most Meiji-era structures were destroyed in Allied firebombing in 1945, and the current Kyuden dates to 1968.

tips.text: The inner grounds are closed to the public except for reserved guided tours (Tuesday-Saturday) and two annual open days, January 2 and February 23.

records.name: Imperial Palace East Gardens
records.description: A 21-hectare public garden built on the former Honmaru, Ninomaru, and Sannomaru grounds of Edo Castle, part of the Imperial Palace complex. The modern garden was built between 1961 and 1968 and opened to the public on October 1, 1968; it includes the Suwa-no-chaya teahouse and the Museum of the Imperial Collections.

tips.text: Free admission; enter via the Otemon, Hirakawamon, or Kitahanebashimon gates.
Closed Mondays and Fridays (except national holidays); hours extend to 9:00-17:00 from April 15 through August.

records.hours: 9:00-16:30 (last entry 16:00); 9:00-17:00 (last entry 16:30) from April 15 to end of August

records.name: Nijubashi Bridge
records.description: Twin bridges spanning the moat in front of the Imperial Palace's Kyuden Plaza, connecting the Kokyo Gaien outer garden to the palace grounds. The stone bridge in front and the iron bridge behind it form one of the most photographed views of the Imperial Palace; ambassadors cross it when presenting credentials to the Emperor.

records.name: Kokyo Gaien National Garden
records.description: The outer garden of the Imperial Palace, a roughly one-square-kilometer national garden administered by Japan's Ministry of the Environment. It preserves moats, gates, bridges, watchtowers, and stone walls from Edo Castle, along with the Statue of Kusunoki Masashige and Wadakura Fountain Park. The garden opened to the public on June 1, 1949.

tips.text: Kokyogaien Service Center can be reached at 03-3231-5509 for visitor information.

records.name: Otemon Gate
records.description: The main historical entrance to Edo Castle and today the principal public entrance to the Imperial Palace East Gardens. It functioned as the main gate during the reign of Tokugawa Hidetada, was damaged in WWII air raids, and has since been repaired; it survives as one of eleven extant Edo Castle gates.

records.name: Sakuradamon Gate
records.description: A gate in the inner moat of the Imperial Palace grounds, one of eleven surviving Edo Castle gates. It is the site of the 1860 Sakuradamon Incident, in which Tairo Ii Naosuke was assassinated by samurai of the Mito and Satsuma domains outside the gate, and of a 1932 assassination attempt on Emperor Hirohito's procession.

records.name: Tayasumon Gate
records.description: A historic gate at the entrance to Kitanomaru Park, constructed in 1685 as part of Edo Castle's outer defenses. It remains one of the eleven surviving original Edo Castle gates.

records.name: Statue of Kusunoki Masashige
records.description: A solid bronze equestrian statue of 14th-century samurai Kusunoki Masashige, who supported Emperor Go-Daigo's attempt to restore imperial power and died by seppuku rather than face capture. Sculpted by Takamura Koun and Goto Sadayuki, the statue was completed and presented to the Imperial Household Agency in 1900 and stands in Kokyo Gaien National Garden overlooking Nijubashi Bridge.

records.name: Wadakura Fountain Park
records.description: A fountain park within Kokyo Gaien National Garden, built in 1961 to commemorate the wedding of Emperor Emeritus Akihito and renovated in 1995 for the marriage of the current Emperor. The three fountain jets form the shape of the chrysanthemum imperial crest; the central jet reaches 8.5 meters and the waterfall is 5.5 meters high and 30 meters wide. It was designed by landscape architect Tsuyoshi Tamura.

records.name: Kitanomaru Park
records.description: A public park just north of the Imperial Palace, on land that was the northernmost section of Edo Castle and later a medicinal garden and residential compound for the Tokugawa family. Created in 1969 and operated by the Ministry of the Environment, it covers about 193,000 square meters and contains the Nippon Budokan, the Science Museum, and the National Museum of Modern Art, Tokyo, along with the historic Tayasumon and Shimizumon gates.

records.name: Nippon Budokan
records.description: An indoor arena in Kitanomaru Park built for judo at the 1964 Summer Olympics, completed September 15, 1964. It seats up to 14,471 people and became internationally famous as a live-album recording venue after The Beatles performed five shows there in 1966; it hosted Shinzo Abe's state funeral in September 2022.

tips.text: The venue is about 2 minutes' walk from Kudanshita Station.

records.name: National Museum of Modern Art, Tokyo
records.description: Japan's first national art museum, established in 1952 and dedicated to 20th-century Japanese art, including Western-style and Nihonga painting. It holds about 8,000 ukiyo-e woodblock prints from the Matsukata collection; the current building was designed by architect Kunio Maekawa.

tips.text: Open Tue-Thu and Sun 10:00-17:00, Fri-Sat 10:00-20:00 (last entry 30 minutes before closing); closed Mondays.

records.name: Science Museum, Tokyo
records.description: A hands-on science and technology museum in Kitanomaru Park, opened in 1964 by the Japan Science Foundation. Exhibits span four floors and about 20 themes including cars, manufacturing, electricity, energy, and information technology, with daily experiment shows and workshops.

tips.text: General admission is 950 yen; last entry is 50 minutes before closing.

records.name: National Archives of Japan
records.description: An institution preserving Japanese government documents and historical records dating back to the Edo period, formally established in July 1971 (predecessor cabinet libraries existed from 1873). It became an Independent Administrative Institution in 2001 and offers a bilingual digital gallery of scrolls, maps, and photographs through the Japan Center for Asian Historical Records.

records.name: Yasukuni Shrine
records.description: A Shinto shrine founded by Emperor Meiji in June 1869 to commemorate those who died in service to Japan, from the Boshin War through the Pacific War. It enshrines over 2.4 million names, including convicted Class-A war criminals, making it a persistent source of diplomatic controversy; sitting prime ministers rarely visit, and no emperor has visited since 1975.

tips.text: The shrine grounds are open daily, 6:00-18:00 (6:00-17:00 in winter months); hours may change for festivals and rituals.

records.name: Yushukan War Memorial Museum
records.description: A military and war history museum on the grounds of Yasukuni Shrine, first inaugurated in 1882; the current building opened July 13, 2002. It displays wills, relics, and historical materials related to those enshrined at Yasukuni and has drawn international criticism for its portrayal of Japan's wartime actions.

records.name: Chidorigafuchi
records.description: A moat on the northwest side of the Imperial Palace, also called Hanzo Moat, named for walls whose shape resembles plovers (chidori). British diplomat Ernest Satow planted the first cherry trees along the moat in 1881; today about 260 cherry trees line a roughly 700-meter promenade, drawing over a million visitors each spring. Rowboat rentals operate seasonally from March to November.

tips.text: Boat rentals are available seasonally from March to November.

records.name: National Diet Building
records.description: The seat of Japan's bicameral legislature, completed November 7, 1936, and built entirely from Japanese materials apart from the stained glass, door locks, and pneumatic tubes. Its central pyramid-shaped tower made it Japan's tallest building from 1936 to 1964. The House of Representatives occupies the south wing and the House of Councillors the north wing.

tips.text: The House of Representatives offers free English-language tours Mondays at 14:00 and Tue-Fri at 15:00, by advance reservation; no tours on weekends, holidays, or Dec 29-Jan 3.

records.name: National Diet Library
records.description: Japan's national library, established in 1948 to support policy research for the Diet and open to the general public as well as Diet members. The Tokyo Main Library opened in 1961 and holds tens of millions of items, including specialized collections on modern political and constitutional history and postwar occupation-era documents.

tips.text: Visitors must be 18 or older to use the Tokyo Main Library reading rooms.

records.name: Supreme Court of Japan
records.description: Japan's highest court, established in 1947 under Article 81 of the Constitution with the power of judicial review. The current building, completed in 1974, is built of steel-reinforced concrete and Japanese white granite with five above-ground and two below-ground floors; the court sits as three five-member Petty Benches or, for constitutional questions, as a 15-member Grand Bench.

records.name: Hibiya Park
records.description: A roughly 16-hectare public park that opened on June 1, 1903, one of Tokyo's first Western-style parks. It was the site of the 1905 Hibiya riots protesting the Treaty of Portsmouth, and is home to a Gothic-style 1929 hall (Hibiya Kokaido) and a 500-year-old ginkgo tree preserved during the park's original construction.

records.name: Hibiya Library and Museum
records.description: A combined library, museum, and lecture facility in Hibiya Park operated by Chiyoda City, offering reading rooms alongside history and culture exhibitions.

records.name: Tokyo Station (Marunouchi Building)
records.description: The main inter-city rail terminal in Tokyo, handling over 4,000 trains and more than 500,000 passengers daily. The historic red-brick Marunouchi building, designed by architect Tatsuno Kingo, opened December 20, 1914; damaged in the May 1945 firebombing and rebuilt with a simplified two-story roofline, it was restored to its pre-war three-story domed appearance in a renovation completed October 2012. The Tokyo Station Gallery art museum occupies the North Dome.

records.name: Marunouchi Building
records.description: A 37-story, 180-meter skyscraper completed in 2002 in the Marunouchi business district, replacing a nine-story 1923 building that had survived the Great Kanto Earthquake and WWII bombings; one portico of the original structure was preserved in the new building. With over 60,000 square meters of floor area it was the largest office building in Asia when it opened, and it houses offices, restaurants, and retail across its floors.

records.name: KITTE
records.description: A retail and dining complex in the JP Tower skyscraper, adjacent to Tokyo Station's Marunouchi side, opened to the public March 21, 2013. It preserves the low-rise frontage of the 1931 Tokyo Central Post Office building, designed by Tetsuro Yoshida, and centers on a triangular glass-roofed atrium surrounded by roughly 100 shops. A rooftop garden overlooks the Marunouchi station building and platforms.

tips.text: Free entry to the complex; hours vary by floor, store, and facility, with irregular closures.

records.name: Intermediatheque
records.description: A free museum on the 2nd and 3rd floors of KITTE, jointly operated by Japan Post and the University Museum of the University of Tokyo. It permanently displays academic specimens, antique scientific instruments, and research materials collected by the university since its founding in 1877.

records.name: Mitsubishi Ichigokan Museum
records.description: An art museum specializing in 19th-century Western art, housed in a faithful brick-by-brick recreation of an 1894 Marunouchi office building designed by British architect Josiah Conder; the original was demolished in 1968 and the museum reopened on the site April 6, 2010. It holds the Maurice Joyant collection of more than 200 works by Henri Toulouse-Lautrec and mounts special exhibitions across roughly 800 square meters of gallery space.

records.name: Idemitsu Museum of Arts
records.description: A museum built around collector Sazo Idemitsu's holdings, founded in 1966 on the 9th floor of the Teigeki Building in Marunouchi. Its roughly 15,000 cultural properties include 2 National Treasures and 57 Important Cultural Properties, among them the Ban Dainagon Ekotoba scroll. The museum has been temporarily closed since December 25, 2024 due to demolition and reconstruction of the Teigeki Building, with no reopening date announced.

tips.text: The museum is temporarily closed since December 25, 2024 for building demolition and reconstruction; check before visiting.

records.name: Tokyo International Forum
records.description: A multi-purpose exhibition and convention center designed by architect Rafael Vinoly, built on the former site of Tokyo City Hall and completed in 1996-97. Its glass-and-steel Glass Hall is shaped like an elongated boat; the complex includes a 5,000-seat hall plus seven additional halls, and hosted weightlifting and powerlifting at the 2020 Olympics and Paralympics.

tips.text: The complex is scheduled to close for large-scale renovation from January 1, 2029 to March 31, 2030.

records.name: Kanda Myojin (Kanda Shrine)
records.description: A Shinto shrine dating to 730 CE, enshrining the kami Daikokuten, Ebisu, and Taira no Masakado. The current structure dates to 1934 and survived the WWII firebombing; the shrine is popular with visitors from nearby Akihabara, including for talismans marketed for blessing electronics, and hosts the Kanda Matsuri, one of Tokyo's three major Shinto festivals, in odd-numbered years around May 15.

records.name: Nikolai-do (Holy Resurrection Cathedral)
records.description: The main cathedral of the Japanese Orthodox Church, founded by Archbishop Nicholas (Kasatkin) and completed March 8, 1891, on a hill at Kanda Surugadai. Designed initially by Josiah Conder and Mikhail Shchurupov in Byzantine Revival style, its bell tower and dome collapsed in the 1923 Great Kanto earthquake; the cathedral was rebuilt and re-consecrated in 1929 to a design by Shinichiro Okada. It was designated a Nationally Important Cultural Property in 1962.

records.name: Jimbocho Book Town
records.description: A concentration of secondhand bookstores in the Kanda-Jinbocho district, one of the world's oldest and largest surviving book towns. As of 2021 the area held about 176 used bookstores, roughly a third of Japan's secondhand book trade, spread along Yasukuni-dori and Hakusan-dori; the district also hosts the headquarters of major publishers including Shogakukan, Shueisha, and Iwanami Shoten, and survived WWII bombing largely intact.

records.name: Meiji University Museum
records.description: A free museum on Meiji University's Surugadai campus combining three collections: a Commodity Department of traditional Japanese crafts such as lacquerware, dyed textiles, and ceramics; a Criminal Materials Department covering the history of crime and punishment, with artifacts including a guillotine and an iron maiden alongside Japanese items; and an Archaeology Department displaying prehistoric-to-tumulus-period finds, including four designated Important Cultural Properties.
records.hours: 10:00-17:00 daily, including Sundays and national holidays

records.name: Akihabara Electric Town
records.description: A shopping district centered on Akihabara Station, administratively within Chiyoda Ward's Sotokanda and Kanda-Sakumacho areas, known as the center of Japanese otaku culture. It earned the nickname 'Electric Town' as a household appliance market in the 1950s before shifting toward computers, video games, anime, and manga in the 1980s.

records.name: Meiji Seimei Kan
records.description: A Greek Revival office building in Marunouchi designed by Shinichiro Okada and completed in March 1934, two years after his death. It survived WWII bombing and was requisitioned by GHQ/SCAP after the war before returning to the Meiji Insurance Company in 1956. In 1997 it became the first Showa-era building designated a National Important Cultural Property; its ground and second floors, with conference and dining rooms, are open to public tours.

tips.text: First and second floors are open to the public for touring; last entry 30 minutes before closing.

records.name: National Showa Memorial Museum (Showakan)
records.description: A national museum near Kudanshita Station, managed by the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare, documenting the lifestyles and hardships of Japanese people during and after World War II. It opened March 27, 1999, partly due to lobbying by the Japan War-Bereaved Families Association, in a building designed by architect Kiyonori Kikutake; the permanent exhibit displays about 450 relics alongside an audio-visual room and library.

tips.text: Admission is 400 yen; closed Mondays and New Year holidays; last entry 30 minutes before closing.

records.name: Hie Shrine
records.description: A Shinto shrine dedicated to Oyamakui no Kami, founded in 1478 by Ota Dokan and rebuilt at its current Nagatacho location in 1659 after the Great Fire of Meireki; the present structure dates to a 1958 postwar reconstruction. It holds one National Treasure sword and 14 Important Cultural Assets, hosts the Sanno Matsuri each June 15 (one of Edo's three great festivals), and is a popular Shichi-Go-San destination, with a hillside approach lined by torii gates and assisted by escalators.

records.name: National Theatre of Japan
records.description: A performing arts complex dedicated to traditional Japanese theatre, operated by the Japan Arts Council and opened in 1966. Its exterior recalls the ancient azekura-zukuri storehouse style; the Large Theatre (1,610 seats) hosts kabuki and classical dance, a Small Hall hosts bunraku and traditional music, and the Engei Hall hosts rakugo and manzai. The complex has been closed for a reconstruction project that began in October 2023.

tips.text: The theatre is closed for reconstruction as of the article's most recent update, following the project's October 2023 start; check current status before visiting.

records.name: Museum of the Imperial Collections
records.description: A museum on the grounds of the Imperial Palace East Gardens displaying imperial household treasures, established in 1993 after the Imperial family donated 6,000 works of art to the Japanese government in 1989. The collection now totals about 9,500 pieces. The original building closed in 2019; a new building's first phase reopened in 2023, with an expansion increasing exhibition space eightfold due to complete in 2026.

tips.text: The museum has been undergoing phased reconstruction since 2019; check current opening status before visiting.
